account:
Lantern Gate followed an earlier venue incident in which duplicate-looking scans appeared after an access-point restart and door staff reverted to paper counts. That report was observational and did not establish the restart as the cause.

Contributor 01 first offered to own offline reconciliation, then the brief assigned them reconciliation design and service implementation; Contributor 06 owned firmware and Contributor 03 owned rollout and training. The offer and assignment establish scope, not delivery, and Contributor 01 explicitly depended on device engineering for retry behaviour.

Contributor 01 designed the reconciliation model around device event IDs, idempotent repeated uploads, retained audit events and deterministic server-receipt ordering, then corrected the wording so receipt order was not presented as historical truth and drafted operator states requiring supervisor verification rather than accusation. Device clocks had multi-minute drift; receipt order was only a deterministic admission rule, not proof of who arrived first.

Contributor 01 implemented the replay-safe event ledger, idempotency key, migration and repeated/interrupted-request tests, then added the reviewer-requested overlapping-batch test and moved response reconstruction inside the transaction. That first service change deliberately excluded conflict selection; the overlapping-batch test only established behaviour around the tested constraint.

After Contributor 05 found that unknown tickets would be misclassified and inflate conflict counts, Contributor 01 fixed validity checking, added the supplied fixture, split invalid/repeated-upload/competing-admit metrics, and delivered conflict classification, clock-offset capture and the console API. Contributor 05 supplied the diagnosis; Contributor 01 supplied the correction and service-side implementation.

When Contributor 06 reported roughly three hours of busy-door retention, Contributor 01 capped claims at two hours, requested oldest-event-age telemetry, and documented queue depth as the temporary signal in a draft runbook covering outage, reconnect, verification and rollback. Event-age telemetry was not in the first firmware build; Contributor 01's cap and warning were initially plans, and operations later owned the final procedure and delivery.

Contributor 01 diagnosed a 20-device load rehearsal bottleneck, replaced full-history recalculation with a locked current-decision row, added contention tests, and reduced the agreed pilot-batch drain from 14 minutes to under 90 seconds. Contributor 07 approved this only for pilot scale: 20 devices and one reconnect wave did not establish large-venue capacity. Evaluation source was written by Contributor 01.

Contributor 08 implemented the conflict-list UI, filters and detail panel using Contributor 01's API and copy; Contributor 01 did not build the console UI, and Contributor 03 owned operational procedure and delivery. Layout and accessibility changes also came from console review, so the visible console was shared work.

In Venue A's 17-minute outage, 1,842 events queued across 12 devices and later uploaded while validation continued; the ledger recorded 31 repeated uploads and six competing-device scans, staff checked all six, and the shift log reported no confirmed double admission. This was one pilot shift; absence from the shift log does not prove no double admission occurred. Evaluation source was written by Contributor 03.

After a Venue A supervisor mistook 'accepted' for arrival-order proof, Contributor 01 completed a presentation-only change to 'selected by system' and added an inline receipt-order explanation; Venue B staff later used it for two online cross-device scans and said the wording was clearer. Venue B had no outage, so this follow-up says little about offline recovery; the change did not alter reconciliation logic. Evaluation sources were written by Contributor 10, Contributor 11.

The pilot review credited Contributor 01 with leading service implementation, recommended retaining the feature at Venues A and B, and the project later enabled three additional small venues after Contributor 06 shipped oldest-event-age telemetry, which Contributor 01 reviewed against the service contract. Firmware implementation and device tests were Contributor 06's; this was a controlled small-venue extension, not a large-hall or estate-wide rollout. Evaluation source was written by Contributor 03.

Across the three added venues, two brief outages produced 2,406 queued events; uploads completed without operator intervention, four conflicts were manually checked, and no confirmed double admissions were logged. One device's queue-age value went stale after sleep, so support retained the two-hour fallback; the defect affected warning accuracy rather than retention or upload, remained under investigation, and larger-venue adoption was undecided at the horizon. Evaluation source was written by Contributor 03.
